Ohio municipal income tax withholding for employers in 2026
An Ohio employer located or doing business in a municipality that imposes an income tax must withhold that tax from the qualifying wages its employees earn there, at that municipality’s rate, unless an exception in Ohio Revised Code section 718.011, such as the 20-day rule, relieves it of withholding. Municipal withholding is a separate duty from Ohio state and school district income tax withholding, and each municipality, or the agency that collects for it, administers the tax.
Do I have to withhold municipal income tax from my Ohio employees’ pay?
An Ohio employer located or doing business in a municipality that imposes an income tax withholds municipal income tax from the qualifying wages its employees earn in that municipality, at that municipality’s rate. Each municipality sets its own rate, so an employer applies a different rate for each municipality, and Ohio has no statewide municipal rate. Exceptions in Ohio Revised Code section 718.011, such as the 20-day rule, relieve the employer of withholding on some wages.


These rules come from Ohio Revised Code (R.C.) chapter 718, including R.C. 718.03 on the duty to withhold. Municipal withholding is separate from state and school district withholding, which the Ohio Department of Taxation (ODT) administers.
Which municipality do I withhold for when an employee works in more than one?
For an employee who works in more than one taxing municipality, an employer that is not a small employer withholds for the municipality of the employee’s principal place of work from the first day, and for each other municipality only where the 20-day rule does not relieve the employer.


R.C. 718.011 defines the principal place of work as the fixed location to which the employee is required to report on a regular and ordinary basis. If there is no fixed location, it is the worksite location in Ohio to which the employee is required to report regularly, and if there is none, it is the location in Ohio where the employee spends the greatest number of days in a calendar year performing services for the employer. A fixed location is a permanent place of doing business in Ohio, such as an office, warehouse, storefront or similar location owned or controlled by the employer. A small employer instead withholds on all of an employee’s qualifying wages for the municipality where its fixed location is.
What is the 20-day rule for municipal income tax withholding, and when does it not apply?
Under the 20-day rule in R.C. 718.011, an employer is not required to withhold municipal income tax on wages for services an employee performs in a municipality on 20 or fewer days in a calendar year, unless the employee’s principal place of work is there, the employee works at a presumed worksite there, the resident employee asks for withholding, or the employee is a professional athlete, entertainer or public figure.


A presumed worksite is a construction site or other temporary worksite where the employer provides services that can reasonably be expected to last more than 20 days in a calendar year. A day counts in a municipality only if the employee spent more time performing services there that day than in any other municipality, and travel to the first work location of the day, between work locations, and certain pick-up and delivery travel is treated as time at the principal place of work.


Once an employee’s days in a municipality exceed 20 in a calendar year, the employer withholds and remits to that municipality for the later days on which it pays qualifying wages for services there. The employer may elect to withhold for the first 20 days as well. If the principal place of work is in a taxing municipality, the 20-day exception applies only if the employer withholds and remits tax on those wages to the municipality where that place is located. The 20-day rule is also subject to the small employer rule, and it does not apply to the extent a tax administrator and the employer have an agreement on how the employer complies with R.C. 718.03.
Does the small employer rule change where I withhold?
An employer with total revenue under $500,000 in the preceding taxable year is a small employer and withholds municipal income tax on all of an employee’s qualifying wages for the municipality where its fixed location is, regardless of how many days the employee works elsewhere.


A small employer remits that tax only to the municipality where its fixed location is, according to R.C. 718.011. As of November 2026, R.C. 718.01 defines total revenue as receipts of any type reported for federal income tax purposes or under generally accepted accounting principles. Governments, including the federal government, states and political subdivisions, are not small employers.
How does an employee who works from home affect municipal withholding?
For municipal withholding, R.C. 718.011 defines a worksite location to exclude the home of an employee. ODT’s Municipal Sites page says that in most cases questions about municipal income taxes should be directed to the city or village that enacted the tax or to the agency that administers the tax on the municipality’s behalf.


ODT’s filing requirements FAQ addresses state income tax separately. It says an employer with an employee working from home in Ohio is transacting business in Ohio and must withhold Ohio income tax, and that answer covers state income tax only.
Should I also withhold for the city where the employee lives?
An employer may withhold municipal income tax for the municipality where an employee lives when the employee asks it to. Tax withheld at the employee’s request when not otherwise required counts as tax required to be withheld, according to R.C. 718.03.


The withholding R.C. 718.03 requires is tied to qualifying wages earned in the municipality.
Which pay counts as qualifying wages for municipal withholding?
Qualifying wages for municipal withholding are wages as defined in section 3121(a) of the Internal Revenue Code, without regard to wage limitations, adjusted as R.C. 718.01 provides.


The statute’s deductions include amounts under a section 125 cafeteria plan, disability payments on account of sickness or accident paid by a party unrelated to the employer, and exempt income. Among the amounts it adds back are employee contributions and deferrals described in sections 401(k), 403(b) and 457, so those deferrals stay in the municipal wage base. School district income tax uses the Ohio withholding wage base instead, which is a different base from the municipal one.


Withholding on tips and gratuities applies only to the extent they are under the employer’s control, meaning paid to the employer for remittance or paid by credit card, debit card or other electronic means, according to R.C. 718.03.
How do I find the municipal tax rate for an employee’s work address?
ODT’s The Finder returns municipal income tax rates for a street address and a date, so an employer can enter the address where the employee works to see the rate for that work location.


The results also list school district income tax rates for the address. Because R.C. 718.03 ties withholding to wages earned in the municipality, the work address is the one to search for the municipal rate on those wages (a small employer searches the address of its fixed location instead), and the employee’s home address is the one to search for the school district.


Neither the State of Ohio nor ODT assumes liability for errors or omissions in the results, and ODT recommends verifying the information with the appropriate municipality or county auditor even if no tax liability is indicated.
How do I register for municipal withholding in Ohio?
Municipal withholding is administered by each municipality or the agency that collects for it, so the Ohio Business Gateway’s municipal page tells employers to contact the municipality for registration information.


ODT’s Municipal Sites page links to the cities and villages that have enacted a municipal individual income tax and says that in most cases questions about these taxes should be directed to the city or village that enacted the tax or to the agency that administers the tax on the municipality’s behalf. A municipality may administer its tax itself or through an agency such as the Regional Income Tax Agency or the Central Collection Agency, which says it collects municipal income taxes for the City of Cleveland and surrounding communities.
Can the state file and pay my municipal withholding for me?
Ohio’s centralized filing with the Department of Taxation covers the municipal net profit tax, not employer withholding, according to ODT’s municipal net profit tax page.


R.C. 718.051 lets an employer report and remit municipal income tax withheld from qualifying wages through the Ohio business gateway, and says this does not affect the due dates. The same section says the state is not a party to the administration of municipal income tax and that municipalities keep their authority to administer, audit and enforce it.
How often do I remit municipal withholding, and when is the annual return due?
Ohio municipal withholding is remitted monthly, within 15 days after month end, when the employer’s withholding for that municipality exceeded $2,399 in the preceding calendar year or $200 in any month of the preceding calendar quarter, and otherwise quarterly, by the last day of the month following the quarter; a municipality may require more frequent remittance.


As of November 2026, R.C. 718.03 lets a municipality require semimonthly remittance, due the third banking day after the 15th or after month end, if the employer’s total for the preceding calendar year exceeded $11,999 or any month of the preceding calendar year exceeded $1,000. The tests are measured for each municipality separately.


On or before the last day of February each year, the employer files a withholding reconciliation return with the tax administrator. It lists the employees from whom tax was or should have been withheld for that municipality in the preceding year, the tax withheld, total qualifying wages, and the information required on Form W-2. ODT sets the state and school district due dates separately.
What happens if I fail to withhold or remit Ohio withholding tax?
An employer is liable for tax it was required to withhold, and Ohio law attaches interest and penalties on the municipal side and on the state and school district side.


For municipal withholding, R.C. 718.03 makes an employer, agent or payer required to withhold liable for the amount required to be withheld whether or not it was withheld, and treats withheld amounts as held in trust for the municipality until remitted. The officer or employee in control of or charged with withholding, filing and paying is personally liable for failure to file or pay. Under R.C. 718.27, a municipality may impose interest on unpaid withholding tax at the federal short-term rate, rounded to the nearest whole percent, plus 5 percent. It may also impose a penalty not exceeding 50 percent of the amount not timely paid and a penalty not exceeding $25 for each failure to timely file a return other than an estimated return, which it must abate or refund on the first failure after the return is filed.


For state and school district withholding, ODT’s 2026 filing guidelines say interest runs from the return due date until the tax is paid, at 7 percent for calendar year 2026, and ODT’s interest-rate table lists 7.0 percent for 2027 for most taxes. As of November 2026, the penalty for failing to file by the due date is the greater of $50 per month up to $500, or 5 percent per month up to 50 percent of the tax. The penalty for failing to pay is 10 percent of the delinquent payment plus double the applicable interest, and tax withheld but not remitted carries 50 percent of the delinquent payment plus double the applicable interest. The same amounts apply to school district withholding. The officer or employee responsible for filing the return and making payment is personally liable for failure to file or pay.
Do I also have to withhold school district income tax, and does it depend on where the employee works?
An employer must withhold Ohio school district income tax for any employee who lives in a taxing school district, whether or not the employer has any operations in that district. ODT’s 2026 filing guidelines say the requirement follows the employee’s address of residence. ODT’s filing requirements FAQ says an employer cannot leave school district tax to an employee’s estimated payments.


Under R.C. 5747.06, the employer must request each employee’s school district of residence, and the employee must furnish correct information and update it. If the employer asked and the employee fails to furnish sufficient and correct information, the employer is not required to withhold school district tax and is not subject to penalties and interest for failing to do so. The employer starts withholding when the employee submits an IT 4 naming the district and need not go back to January, according to ODT’s filing requirements FAQ.


Traditional tax base districts withhold on the same wage base and number of exemptions as Ohio withholding, at the district’s rate. Earned income only tax base districts withhold at a flat rate with no reduction for personal exemptions, so one flat percentage cannot serve every district. ODT’s school district rate sheet lists the 2026 rates. Employers remit school district tax on the SD 101, not the IT 501.
How do I register for Ohio state income tax withholding and file the returns?
An employer required to withhold Ohio income tax must register within 15 days of when that liability begins, through OH|TAX eServices, and must file and pay electronically.


Every employer maintaining an office or transacting business in Ohio and paying compensation to an employee, resident or nonresident, must withhold Ohio income tax, according to ODT’s 2026 filing guidelines. The guidelines list situations where withholding is not required, including agricultural labor, domestic service in a private home, and residents of Michigan, Indiana, Kentucky, West Virginia or Pennsylvania earning compensation for services provided in Ohio. Registration takes the employer’s FEIN, the legal name of the business and an email address. One withholding account number covers both Ohio withholding and school district withholding.


Each employee completes Form IT 4, or the employer withholds on the basis of zero exemptions. The employer keeps the IT 4 for at least four years and does not send it to ODT. ODT’s FAQ says the IT 4 does not apply to municipal income tax. ODT’s Employer Withholding page lists withholding tables effective August 1, 2026 and a 2.75 percent rate on supplemental compensation such as bonuses.


ODT sets each employer’s filing frequency every calendar year from the combined state and school district tax withheld, or required to be withheld, in the 12-month period ending June 30 of the preceding calendar year. As of November 2026, the tiers are as follows.


Filing frequency

$84,000 or more

Partial-weekly filers file school district withholding monthly. An employer’s initial filing frequency is set during registration, and an employer that registered on or after July 1 of the preceding calendar year remits quarterly unless ODT notifies it otherwise. If the combined Ohio and school district tax withheld in a pay period reaches $100,000 or more, the Ohio income tax portion is due by the first banking day after the payroll date. ODT’s 2026 due date schedule lists November 16, 2026 for the October monthly period, December 15, 2026 for November, January 15 of the following year for December, and February 1 of the following year for the fourth quarter. The IT 941 and SD 141 annual reconciliations are due January 31 of the following tax year, and total tax withheld must equal the W-2s and 1099s the employer submits through OH|TAX eServices.
What are Ohio’s new employer unemployment tax rate and taxable wage base?
For 2026, Ohio’s annual taxable wage base for unemployment tax is $9,000 per employee, and a new employer’s rate is 2.85 percent including a 0.15 percent technology and customer service fee, or 5.85 percent including the same fee for a construction employer, according to the Ohio Department of Job and Family Services (ODJFS) 2026 rate sheet.
How do I register for Ohio unemployment tax, and when are quarterly reports due?
An Ohio employer reports its own unemployment tax liability to the Ohio Department of Job and Family Services as soon as one or more employees are in covered employment, online through The SOURCE (State of Ohio Unemployment Resource for Claimants and Employers) or on the Report to Determine Liability (JFS 20100), according to ODJFS’s employer obligations page.


As of November 2026, a regular for-profit employer is subject to Ohio’s unemployment compensation law if it had at least one individual in employment for some portion of a day in each of 20 different calendar weeks in the current or preceding calendar year, or paid wages of $1,500 or more in any calendar quarter in either year, according to R.C. 4141.011. A nonprofit uses a different test, at least four individuals in employment for some portion of a day in each of 20 weeks.


Registration with ODJFS is separate from the ODT withholding account.


Employers subject to the law file quarterly wage reports electronically, even if they had no workers or paid no wages in a quarter. Per ODJFS’s new employer page, the reports are due April 30, July 31, October 31 and January 31, and the next business day when the date falls on a weekend.
Do I have to report new hires to the State of Ohio?
Ohio employers report each new hire to the Ohio New Hire Reporting Center within 20 days of the hire date. R.C. 3121.893 sets the 20-day limit, and the Ohio New Hire Reporting Center says employers also report every independent contractor working in Ohio within 20 days.


A newly hired employee is one not previously employed by the employer, or previously employed but separated for at least 60 consecutive days.


As of November 2026, Ohio Administrative Code 5101:12-10-90.1 sets a civil penalty of $25 for each failure to make a report, and $500 for each failure that results from a conspiracy between the employer and the employee not to supply the report or to supply a false or incomplete one.
Do I need Ohio workers’ compensation coverage through the Bureau of Workers’ Compensation (BWC)?
Ohio law requires an employer with one or more employees to have workers’ compensation coverage; the Bureau of Workers’ Compensation’s coverage application (U-3) carries a $120 non-refundable fee, and BWC bases the annual premium on reported payroll. As of November 2026, BWC’s getting coverage page states the coverage requirement and the application fee.


BWC requires a new application from employers with one or more full or part-time employees, independent contractors and subcontractors with employees, corporations with multiple owner-officers, out-of-state employers bringing employees to work in Ohio for 90 consecutive days or more, and certain domestic household employers. Ohio law requires coverage from the date the employer first hires employees in Ohio.


BWC sets an estimated annual premium at the start of a policy period. At the end of the policy year the employer files a true-up report of actual payroll online. For private employers the true-up period begins July 1 and the deadline is August 31, and for public employers it begins January 1 and the deadline is February 28, according to BWC’s true-up report page.
